Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD is a standard binary package for Arch Linux that downloads a pre-built tarball from the project's own GitHub releases page. The `source` array contains a single HTTPS URL from `github.com/OpenWhispr/openwhispr`, which is the declared upstream. The global scope contains only standard variable declarations and arrays with no command substitutions or suspicious operations. There is no `pkgver()` function that would execute at sourcing time. The `sha256sums` field contains a real checksum (not SKIP), though a missing checksum would not be grounds to fail this gate anyway since the purpose of these commands is precisely to fetch and extract sources for auditing. The `package()` function is defined but will not execute during `--nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` operations, so its contents are out of scope for this gate.

The PKGBUILD follows conventional AUR binary package practices: it declares metadata, downloads a release artifact from the project's own GitHub, extracts it, and installs files to standard locations. No malicious behavior is present in the portions that would execute during these commands.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard binary AUR package fetching own upstream source</summary>
</security_assessment>

The PKGBUILD is a standard Arch Linux binary package that downloads a prebuilt release tarball from the official GitHub repository (github.com/OpenWhispr/openwhispr/releases). It installs the application to /opt/openwhispr, creates a launcher script in /usr/bin that passes arguments to the binary with the --no-sandbox flag (common for Electron apps when chrome-sandbox is not properly set up), and adds a .desktop entry, icon, and license files. The sha256sums placeholder is noted as being updated by CI via updpkgsums, which is normal practice for -bin packages. No suspicious network requests, obfuscation, eval usage, or file operations outside expected packaging scope are present. The --no-sandbox flag and removal of chrome-sandbox are typical for Electron-based AUR packages and do not indicate malicious intent.
